newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan oil monopoly chief indicted, ministry says.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan oil monopoly chief indicted, ministry says.

text.p: Chang Tzu-yuan, chairman of state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp, was indicted on Friday on charges unrelated to his duties at Taiwan's oil monopoly, the economics ministry said.

"We have learned that he has been indicted on a charge that carries a possible six-year prison term, but we are not sure of the specifics of the allegations against him," a spokesman for the ministry said by telephone.
The ministry was reviewing the matter and would not decide whether to suspend Chang until officials receive formal written notice from prosecutors, the spokesman said.

Officials at Chinese Petroleum confirmed that Chang had been charged, adding that this was in connection to activities allegedly committed during his tenure as mayor of Taiwan's central Taichung city several years ago.
The charges stem from allegations of improprieties in the city government's rezoning of local property, they said.
Further details were not available, officials said.

The indictment was the latest in a string of blows to Taiwan's oil giant, where president Chen Kuo-young resigned on November 19 to take responsibility for a series of explosions, fires and oil spills that cost the company millions of dollars in compensation claims and fines in 1996.

Chinese Petroleum, which reported a huge budget deficit in November, finally saw its fiscal 1996-97 budget adopted by parliament on Thursday after months of political footdragging over its proposed privatisation and other contentious issues.

The budget stalemate and popular opposition have prevented Chinese Petroleum from carrying through oil price increases that would enable it to balance its budget at a time when world oil prices are sharply higher that it had anticipated.

Parliament cut the monopoly's budget for key overseas expansion programmes in Indonesia and Vietnam and cancelled its participation in a consortium planning to build a power station in northern Taiwan.
Chairman Chang has vowed to stay on at Chinese Petroleum despite mounting criticism of his stewardship from lawmakers, government officials and Taiwan's media.
